location: Braymer, Missouri — Farm Scene, Milking Time
recipient: Mrs. R. H. Benney, Lees Summit, Missouri
notes: Real-photo postcard, hand-tinted, stock number “No. 82 — Farm Scene Locals” — a mass-produced generic dairy-farm image overprinted with the caption “Scene near BRAYMER, MO.,” a common practice for small towns that didn’t warrant custom local photography. Front shows a farmer in a straw hat milking a cow beside an open barn door hung with drying corn shocks. Postmarked Braymer, MO, Jun 26, 1923, 6 PM. 1¢ green Washington stamp. Message (best-effort read, cursive is faint): “Dear folks — Hope you are all well. Have been warm. Write a letter before long. Love [to] Sis and every one. Lovingly, your daughter.” Addressed to Mrs. R.H. Benney in Lees Summit, roughly 70 miles southwest — likely a daughter writing home to her mother from a visit or stay near Braymer.
feed_description: A daughter’s quick note home from Braymer, Missouri in June 1923, on a mass-produced “farm scene” postcard overprinted for the local market — hoping folks are well and promising a letter before long.

location: Tallahassee, Florida — Lake Bradford, “The Disappearing Lake”
notes: Published by Asheville Post Card Co., Asheville, N.C., part of their “Beautiful Florida Series,” C.T. American Art-Colored process. Front (card T-15, no. 93714) shows cypress trees draped in Spanish moss standing in Lake Bradford’s still water at dusk. Back caption explains the lake’s local nickname: “the Disappearing Lake, nearly disappears every seven years” — a real characteristic of several lakes in this karst region of North Florida, which periodically drain through underground limestone sinks and refill over time. Postmarked Tallahassee, FL, Jun 10, 1935, 5 PM. Message, addressed to a Boy Scout troop leader: “Dear Scoutmaster. How are you? Hope you are fine. How are the boys doing on the room? Hope they will not disappoint you like we have been doing. As soon as I come back I will bring mine over. Wish you were with me.” Signature obscured by the postmark. Sent to Rev. Wm. Wallace in Wrightsville, a small community near Jacksonville — likely a scout from Wallace’s troop writing during a summer trip or camp near Tallahassee.
feed_description: A scout writes to “Dear Scoutmaster” Rev. Wm. Wallace in June 1935, apologizing for not living up to expectations and promising to make it right — mailed from beside Tallahassee’s Lake Bradford, known locally as “the Disappearing Lake.”

address: Rio Grande Valley, South Texas (near Harlingen/McAllen)
recipient: Mr. Arthur Brauer, 509 Ave of Oaks, Houston 29, Texas
notes: “A Don Bartels color reproduction,” published by Don R. Bartels, 510 N. 7th St., McAllen, Texas (card DB-166, S6276). Front shows a royal-palm-lined South Texas boulevard. Back caption: “South Texas displays many types of beautiful palms to remind you of it's semi-tropical climate. Warm winters and cool summers bring many visitors to this area both winter and summer.” Postmarked Harlingen, Tex., Jun 25, 1957, 3 PM. 3¢ Statue of Liberty “In God We Trust” stamp. Message (best-effort read, cursive is dense): “Tuesday — Dear Art, Just got to Harlingen, going on to Brownsville now, looks like a storm coming on. Everybody is OK. It's WARM. Told old Houston — 509. Hope you are OK — go see the travel agent, please — see you Friday. Love, Helen.” Addressed to Arthur Brauer at 509 Ave of Oaks, Houston 29 (pre-ZIP postal zone number, standard for the era). A quick travel update from the Rio Grande Valley, likely from a road trip working down toward Brownsville and the Mexican border.
feed_description: Helen writes “Dear Art” from Harlingen, Texas in June 1957, mid-road-trip toward Brownsville with a storm rolling in — sent home on a palm-lined South Texas postcard by McAllen photographer Don Bartels.

location: Myrtle Beach, South Carolina — Ocean Plaza Pier
address: Ocean Plaza Pier, North Strand, Myrtle Beach, SC
recipient: Irene Morris, R.D. #1, Canal Fulton, Ohio
notes: “Riviera of the South” — a mid-century marketing nickname for Myrtle Beach. Ektachrome by Justin Plyler, published by Plyler Sales Co., Myrtle Beach, S.C. (card 2204). Front shows a crowded beach day near the Ocean Plaza Pier and North Strand — lifeguard stand, umbrellas, sunbathers. Postmarked Myrtle Beach, Jun 14, 1960, 3 PM. 4¢ Lincoln stamp. Message: “Dear Irene, We are in Myrtle Beach beside the Atlantic Ocean. I went swimming in the Atlantic yesterday. I picked up some sea shells, I'll give you some when I get back later this week. Shirley Long.” Sent to Irene Morris on a rural delivery route in Canal Fulton, Ohio.
feed_description: Shirley Long sends a beach-day update to Irene Morris in Canal Fulton, Ohio — first swim in the Atlantic, sea shells promised for when she's back, June 1960 at Myrtle Beach's Ocean Plaza Pier.

location: Great Smoky Mountains National Park — Loop-Over Underpass
address: U.S. Highway 441 (Newfound Gap Road), Great Smoky Mountains National Park
recipient: Erma Tuggle, 3315 Summit, Apt. 4, Kansas City 11, Missouri
notes: Curteichcolor 3-D Natural Color Reproduction, card N.117, distributed by James S. Bryant Industries, Orangeburg, S.C. Back caption: “The Loop-Over Underpass on U.S. 441 in the Great Smoky Mountains National Park is one of the spectacular engineering features of the Trans-mountain Highway, and a well remembered landmark of the tourist.” The loop is a real feature of the road's climb toward Newfound Gap, where the highway spirals and passes back under itself through a stone-faced tunnel to gain elevation on the steep mountainside. Postmarked Signal Mountain, Tenn. (near Chattanooga, a common gateway stop for Smokies-bound travelers), Apr 20, 1961. 4¢ “First Automated Post Office in the United States” commemorative stamp (honoring the 1960 Providence, R.I. facility). Message, dated 4-20-61 in the sender's hand: “Hi Erma! Having a wonderful time. Been to a lot of places and seen a lot of things. Took a lot of pictures. This country sure is beautiful. So I'll see you later. Bernice.” Sent to Erma Tuggle in Kansas City 11 (pre-ZIP postal zone), Missouri.

feed_description: Bernice writes home mid-road-trip through the Smokies in April 1961, raving about the scenery from a stop near Chattanooga — sent on a card featuring U.S. 441's famous spiraling Loop-Over Underpass.

address: Michigan (general “Fall Color Tour” scene; no specific site named)
year: c. 1955 (estimated from printer's code — card was never mailed)
notes: Photographed and published by Penrod Studio, Berrien Center, Michigan; printed by Dexter Press, Inc., West Nyack, NY (card 7152-C). Front shows a man and small child walking hand-in-hand down a leaf-strewn country road under a full canopy of gold and crimson autumn trees. Back caption: “Scenic roads and trails, beautiful lakes and forests make Michigan's Fall Color Tours an exciting experience.” This card was never mailed — no stamp, no postmark, address side left blank except for the message. A small printed code near the stamp box (“5-6/25”) follows Dexter Press's standard print-date shorthand, which points to a plate/print date of roughly May–June 1955 — offered here as a ballpark rather than a confirmed date, since nothing on the card was ever postmarked. The handwritten message is in Portuguese, not English: roughly, translated — “[This place] isn't exactly like the photograph shows it, but you can get an idea [of what it's like].” A generic state-tourism card, likely picked up by a Portuguese-speaking traveler passing through Michigan and written but never sent.
feed_description: An unmailed “Fall Color Tour” postcard from Michigan, written in Portuguese and never sent — the message admits the photo doesn't quite do the scene justice, but it gives you an idea. Ballparked to the mid-1950s from a printer's code.

year: c. mid-to-late 1950s (postmark day legible, year worn away — see notes)
recipient: Mrs. Elisabeth Pfanneberg, c/o Mimno, 83 Pleasant Street, Lexington 73, Massachusetts, USA
notes: Published by Verlag Heinr. Koch, Essen (card 56272). Black-and-white real-photo card of Bochum's Schauspielhaus (municipal drama theatre) seen across its landscaped park grounds, benches and flowering shrubs in the foreground. Sent airmail (“Mit Luftpost / Par Avion” label) with a 40pf blue Theodor Heuss definitive stamp (West German series issued 1954–1960). Postmark shows a Bochum-area cancellation dated the 31st of May, but the year digit isn’t legible on the scan. Addressed to “Lexington 73” — a pre-ZIP postal zone number (zones were retired when ZIP codes launched in 1963), which narrows the likely date to sometime before then, consistent with the Heuss stamp’s 1954–1960 run. Ballparking it to the mid-to-late 1950s on that basis. Message is written in fast, looping German cursive (closer to old Kurrentschrift style than modern hand) across the full back and margin. Best-effort reading after close inspection: opens with “Liebe Mutti!” (“Dear Mommy!”); the body’s content resists confident word-for-word transcription, but its tone reads as warm, casual family chat — touching on good weather/sunshine and day-to-day activities rather than any specific news. It closes with a “viele liebe Grüße” (“many warm greetings”) sign-off signed by several family members, including what appears to be “Oma” (Grandma) — suggesting a multi-generational family greeting rather than a single letter-writer. Sent to Elisabeth Pfanneberg, care of a “Mimno” household in Lexington, Massachusetts — likely German relatives writing to family who had emigrated to the Boston area. Note: the message body remains only partially deciphered despite repeated close review; a native reader of old German cursive would likely get more out of it than this transcription does.

feed_description: A German family postcard from Bochum's Schauspielhaus, airmailed to Elisabeth Pfanneberg in Lexington, Massachusetts — the German cursive resists full translation, but it's clearly a warm, multi-signature family letter. Ballparked to the mid-to-late 1950s.
